MEDI2200 · Week 6 · Gene Expression I–III

Gene Expression from DNA to protein

How a stretch of DNA becomes a working protein — transcribed into RNA, processed into mature mRNA, then read three bases at a time by the ribosome. This guide follows Prof. Rizos' three lectures end to end, using their own figures.

Covers Parts I–III (RNA · Transcription · Translation) Figures from your lecture slides Self-tests interactive

How to use this guide

Every subsection has a reference code like §4.2 — quote it to go deeper on exactly that piece. Each figure from your slides appears as a numbered Plate with a Label Key decoding what's in it. The coloured tags carry the extras:

Reasoning
The why behind the mechanism — form follows function.
Memory hook
A trick to lock it in for the exam.

Why it matters beyond the diagram.
§0Part I · foundations

The Central Dogma & the chemistry of RNA

Before the machinery, the molecule: what RNA is made of and which way it is built.

Genetic information moves in one main direction — DNA → RNA → protein — a route so universal, from bacteria to humans, that it is called the central dogma of molecular biology. Transcription copies a stretch of DNA into RNA; translation then reads that RNA to build a protein. Some RNAs are the final product and are never translated. Timing matters too: DNA is replicated in S-phase (before a cell divides), whereas transcription happens mostly in G1, after division, when the cell is busy expressing its genes.

§0.1The building block: a ribonucleotide

Every RNA is a chain of ribonucleotides, each one a three-part unit: a ribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. Plate 0.1 dissects a single unit and shows how units connect.

Label Key — reading a nucleotide
Ribose (pentose sugar)
The five-carbon sugar backbone. Its carbons are numbered 1'–5'. The 2'-OH (present on ribose, absent on deoxyribose) is what chemically distinguishes RNA from DNA.
5' carbon → phosphate
The phosphate group hangs off the 5' carbon. This is the "start" end of the strand.
3' carbon → OH
Carries a free hydroxyl. The next nucleotide is added here — which is why RNA is always built 5' → 3'.
Phosphodiester linkage
Joins the 3'-C of one sugar to the 5'-C of the next — the covalent bond that forms the backbone.
Glycosidic bond
Joins the base to the 1' carbon of the sugar.
Pyrimidine bases (uracil, cytosine)
Single-ring bases. RNA uses uracil (U) in place of DNA's thymine.
Purine bases (guanine, adenine)
Larger, two-ring bases.
Reasoning · why 5' → 3', always

Chain growth is defined by chemistry, not convention: the only reactive site for adding a nucleotide is the free 3'-OH at the growing end. A new nucleotide arrives as a triphosphate, and its 5'-phosphate is attacked by that 3'-OH. So the strand can only extend at its 3' end — the reason both transcription and translation have a fixed directionality you will meet again and again.

§0.2Base pairing and shape

  • Same pairing rules as DNA — a pyrimidine always pairs with a purine: A pairs with U, and C pairs with G.
  • RNA is single-stranded — but that single strand folds back on itself, base-pairing internally to build complex 3-D shapes (crucial for tRNA and rRNA function later).
Memory hook · purines vs pyrimidines

PURines are A and G — "Pure As Gold." Everything else (C, U, T) is a pyrimidine. And pyrimidine / CUT — the pyrimidines are C, U, T.

Clinical / real-world · why RNA is fragile

That extra 2'-OH makes RNA far more chemically reactive — and less stable — than DNA. This is exactly why DNA is the cell's archival copy while RNA is a disposable working copy, and why mRNA vaccines must be wrapped in lipid nanoparticles and kept in a cold chain: the naked RNA would otherwise degrade in minutes.

R Recall — foundations
  • Central dogma — DNA → RNA → protein (RNA can be the end product).
  • 5' → 3' — RNA is built by adding to the free 3'-OH.
  • RNA bases — A·U and C·G; uracil replaces thymine; single-stranded but folds.
§1Part I · gene anatomy

Anatomy of a gene

A gene is more than its coding sequence — it is a layout of signals that say where to start, what to keep, and where to stop.

To transcribe a gene correctly the cell must know exactly where to begin, which pieces to keep, and where to end. Those instructions are built into the DNA sequence itself. Plate 1.1 lays out a real human gene — CDKN2A on chromosome 9p21, which encodes the tumour-suppressor protein p16 — from promoter to poly-A site, and shows what survives into the mature mRNA.

Label Key — parts of a gene
Promoter (−300 to −50)
Upstream sequence that recruits the transcription machinery. Sets where and how strongly a gene is switched on.
+1 Transcription start site (TSS)
The first base actually transcribed — the reference point everything else is numbered from.
Exons (1α, 2, 3)
Expressed sequences retained in the mature mRNA.
Introns (1, 2)
Intervening sequences that are transcribed but then spliced out.
5' UTR
Untranslated region at the front of the mRNA — transcribed and kept, but not translated; carries ribosome-loading signals.
3' UTR
Untranslated tail — kept but not translated; holds stability and localisation signals.
Transcription termination sequence
Marks where transcription ends.

Notice what the mRNA at the bottom of Plate 1.1 has lost: the introns are gone and the exons are stitched together. Distal enhancers (not shown on the map) can further crank up transcription from a promoter even when located far away.

§1.1Start and stop signals on the mRNA

Once made, the mRNA carries the punctuation for protein synthesis. Plate 1.2 shows where translation begins and ends.

Label Key — punctuation of the message
AUG — start / initiation codon
Sets the reading frame and codes for methionine; translation begins here.
UAA · UAG · UGA — stop codons
Three "termination" codons; none codes for an amino acid, so each ends translation.
Amino-acid chain
The protein product, read from the codons between start and stop.
Memory hook · the three stop codons

UAA · UAG · UGA — "U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away." All three tell the ribosome to leave.

§1.2Template vs coding strand

DNA is double-stranded, but for any one gene only one strand is read at a time:

  • Template (non-coding) strand — the strand the polymerase actually reads to build the RNA.
  • Coding (non-template) strand — the other strand; its sequence is the same as the new RNA (with T in place of U), which is why it "codes" even though it is not read.
  • The same physical strand can be the template for one gene and the coding strand for its neighbour — direction is per-gene, not per-strand.
Reasoning · why name the strand you don't read the "coding" strand?

It seems backwards, but it is a convenience: when biologists write a gene sequence they quote the coding strand because it reads the same as the mRNA (and therefore the protein). You can translate the coding strand in your head without first flipping it to its complement — so it is the strand that gets printed in databases.

Clinical / real-world · CDKN2A and cancer

The gene mapped in Plate 1.1 is not a random example. CDKN2A encodes p16, a brake on the cell cycle. Loss or mutation of CDKN2A removes that brake and is one of the most common events in melanoma and several other cancers — a reminder that "gene structure" is the substrate on which disease-causing mutations act, whether in the coding exons, the splice sites, or the regulatory promoter.

R Recall — gene anatomy
  • Layout — promoter → TSS(+1) → exons/introns → termination; enhancers act at a distance.
  • Kept vs cut — exons + UTRs stay; introns are spliced out.
  • Codons — AUG starts (Met); UAA/UAG/UGA stop.
  • Strands — template is read; coding strand matches the RNA.
§2Part I · the enzyme

RNA polymerases

The enzymes that read DNA and write RNA — fast, primer-free, and only lightly proofread.

Transcription is carried out by large, multi-subunit enzymes called RNA polymerases. They clamp onto DNA and synthesise RNA, adding free ribonucleotides to the 3' end of the growing strand in the 5' → 3' direction — exactly the chemistry set up in §0.

§2.1How they work

  • No primer needed — unlike DNA polymerase, RNA pol can start a chain from scratch.
  • Energy source — hydrolysis of the incoming ribonucleotide triphosphate (rNTP → rNMP + PPi) drives each addition.
  • Modest proofreading — an error roughly every 104 nucleotides; far less accurate than DNA replication.
  • High processivity — once started, a polymerase tends to finish the whole transcript without falling off.
Reasoning · why the cell tolerates sloppy proofreading

A DNA error is permanent and heritable, so DNA polymerase proofreads obsessively (~1 error in 107). But an mRNA is a disposable copy made in hundreds of identical runs; a rare mistake in one transcript produces one faulty protein that is quickly turned over. The cost of an occasional error is trivial, so evolution never paid the speed penalty of tight proofreading here.

§2.2Three eukaryotic polymerases

Eukaryotes divide the work across three RNA polymerases. They share a similar architecture — a conserved 10-subunit catalytic core, with some subunits shared between them — but transcribe different products in different places.

The three eukaryotic RNA polymerases
FeatureRNA Pol IRNA Pol IIRNA Pol III
LocationNucleolusNucleusNucleus
Main productsPre-rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S)mRNA, snRNA, miRNA5S rRNA, tRNAs, snRNA U6, 7S RNA
Fidelity~10-4~10-4~10-4
No. of subunits141217
Memory hook · who makes what

Count up in order: Pol I → the big ribosomal RNAs (in the nucleolI); Pol II → the messenger (mRNA — the one that matters for genes coding proteins); Pol III → the small stuff, tRNA and 5S. "I ribosomes, II messages, III transfers."

Clinical / real-world · poisoning the polymerase

α-amanitin, the toxin of the death-cap mushroom (Amanita phalloides), specifically blocks RNA Pol II. With mRNA synthesis shut down, protein production collapses — hitting the liver hardest and causing fatal liver failure days after ingestion. In bacteria, the antibiotic rifampicin works the same way against the bacterial RNA polymerase, which is different enough to spare ours — the basis of its selective toxicity in treating tuberculosis.

R Recall — RNA polymerases
  • Behaviour — build 5'→3', no primer, modest proofreading (1/104), high processivity, energy from rNTP hydrolysis.
  • Pol I / II / III — rRNA / mRNA / tRNA + 5S; nucleolus / nucleus / nucleus.
§3Part II · initiation

Transcription initiation

Getting started is the hard part — a whole complex must assemble before the first base is written.

Transcription is a stepwise process, and its most tightly controlled step is initiation. It begins at a defined position — the transcription start site (TSS) — which sits inside a stretch of DNA called the core promoter. The core promoter's job is to assemble the pre-initiation complex (PIC): the general transcription factors plus the RNA polymerase.

§3.1Promoter motifs

Core promoters are recognised through short sequence motifs. A given promoter carries some combination of:

  • TATA box — ~30 bp upstream of the TSS; the classic docking site for the TATA-binding protein.
  • Initiator (Inr) — overlaps the TSS itself and binds TAF1; more common than the TATA box.
  • DPE (downstream promoter element) — increases TFIID binding in TATA-less promoters.
  • BRE — enhances binding of TFIIB to the promoter.
  • CpG islands — GC-rich regions with distinct chromatin marks, often found at genes that are constitutively (always) expressed.

Promoters can be activated from a distance by enhancers, which bind transcription factors (TF) and cofactors (COF) to raise output from the core promoter.

§3.2The pre-initiation complex

Every PIC shares a conserved core, shown assembled in Plate 3.1.

Label Key — who's in the complex
RNA Pol II
The polymerase itself — the enzyme that will make the RNA.
TBP (TATA-binding protein)
Bends and grips the DNA; required even at TATA-less promoters, so it is the universal anchor of the complex. Part of TFIID.
TATA
The core-promoter DNA element TBP sits on.
TFIID
Contains TBP; binds the core promoter first.
TFIIA
Stabilises the TBP–DNA complex.
TFIIB
Recruits RNA Pol II and interacts with TBP; helps set the start site.
TFIIF
Recruits and stabilises Pol II; influences start-site selection.
TFIIE
Recruits and stimulates TFIIH; bridges Pol II and TFIIH.
TFIIH
The active engine: helicase/ATPase activity opens the DNA, and CDK7 kinase activity phosphorylates Pol II to launch it.

§3.3From assembly to escape

The order of events reads like a build sequence: TFIID (via TBP) settles on the core promoter → TFIIA stabilises it → TFIIB brings in Pol II (with TFIIF) → TFIIE recruits TFIIH. TFIIH then uses ATP to unwind the DNA into an open complex, and its CDK7 kinase phosphorylates Pol II, releasing it from the promoter so it can move down the template adding nucleotides to the 3' end. A ~1 MDa complex called Mediator couples distant activator proteins to the polymerase. Pol I and Pol III build their own PICs with their own polymerase-specific factors.

Reasoning · why phosphorylation is the "go" signal

Building the PIC and starting to transcribe are deliberately split into two switches. Assembly positions everything correctly but keeps the polymerase clamped at the promoter. Only when TFIIH's CDK7 phosphorylates the tail of Pol II does the enzyme let go and enter elongation. Making "escape" a separate, enzyme-controlled step gives the cell a final checkpoint — a place to hold a fully-loaded gene poised but silent until the right signal arrives.

Clinical / real-world · TFIIH does two jobs

TFIIH is not only a transcription factor — the same complex is central to nucleotide-excision DNA repair. Inherited mutations in its subunits cause xeroderma pigmentosum and Cockayne syndrome: extreme UV sensitivity, skin cancers and developmental defects. It is a striking example of one machine shared between reading genes and repairing them.

R Recall — initiation
  • Core promoter assembles the PIC at the TSS; motifs = TATA, Inr, DPE, BRE; CpG islands at housekeeping genes.
  • PIC core = Pol II + TBP + GTFs (TFIIA/B/D/E/F/H).
  • TFIIH opens DNA (helicase/ATPase) and phosphorylates Pol II (CDK7) → promoter escape.
  • Enhancers + Mediator connect distant activators to the promoter.
§4Part II · processing

RNA processing

The raw transcript is not yet a usable message — it must be capped, spliced and tailed.

As Pol II transcribes, the growing RNA is already being edited. Three co-transcriptional modifications, all happening in the nucleus, convert the primary transcript into a functional mature mRNA: (1) add a 5' cap, (2) splice out introns and join exons, and (3) add a 3' poly-A tail. Plate 4.4 shows all three on one molecule.

§4.1Step 1 — the 5' cap

When the transcript is only ~25 nucleotides long, a 7-methylguanosine cap is added to its 5' end. Three enzymes act in succession: a phosphatase removes a 5' phosphate, a guanylyl transferase adds GMP through an unusual 5'-to-5' linkage, and a methyl transferase adds methyl groups (methylation of just the guanosine = "cap 0"; methylating the adjacent ribose = "cap 1", and so on).

Label Key — the cap
7-methylguanosine
The capping nucleotide, added backwards onto the 5' end.
5'-to-5' triphosphate link
The unusual bond joining cap to transcript — not the normal 5'→3' backbone, which is what makes the cap chemically distinctive.
Cap-1 / cap-2 methylations
Additional methyl groups on the ribose of the first (and second) transcribed bases.

The cap earns its keep three ways: it distinguishes mRNA from other RNAs, protects the mRNA from degradation, and helps the ribosome attach to begin translation.

§4.2Step 2 — splicing

Both introns and exons are transcribed, so the introns must be cut out and the exons joined. The scale is large: an average human gene has ~8 introns, each with a median length of ~1000 bp, and removing a single intron uses ~five small RNAs and hundreds of proteins. Introns are defined by three short, conserved sites — the 5' splice site, the branch point, and the 3' splice site (Plate 4.2).

Label Key — the three intron signals
5' splice site (GU)
The start of the intron; a near-invariant GU just after the 5' exon.
Branch point (A)
An adenosine ~20–50 bases upstream of the 3' end; its 2'-OH launches the first cut.
Polypyrimidine tract
A C/U-rich stretch that helps recruit the splicing machinery to the 3' site.
3' splice site (AG)
The end of the intron; a near-invariant AG before the 3' exon.

Splicing is catalysed by the spliceosome (small nuclear RNAs that base-pair with those consensus sequences, plus ~100 proteins), in two transesterification reactions:

  1. Branching — the branch-point adenosine attacks the 5' splice site, cutting the 5' exon free and forming a lariat (loop) of intron still attached to the 3' exon.
  2. Exon ligation — the freed 3'-OH of the 5' exon attacks the 3' splice site, joining the two exons and releasing the lariat intron.

On completion the mRNA is released, the lariat intron is degraded, and the spliceosome is recycled. Crucially, splicing the same transcript in different ways — alternative splicing — lets one gene produce several RNA and protein species.

Reasoning · why bother cutting genes into pieces?

Introns look wasteful — why transcribe ~1000-bp stretches only to throw them away? The payoff is alternative splicing: by choosing which exons to keep, one gene can encode many related proteins, vastly expanding the proteome without expanding the genome. It also lets exons — often functional protein modules — be shuffled and recombined over evolution ("exon shuffling"). The intron cost buys combinatorial flexibility.

§4.3Step 3 — cleavage & polyadenylation

Near the 3' end, two factors read out the end signal: CPSF (cleavage/polyadenylation specificity factor) binds the AAUAAA polyadenylation signal, and CstF (cleavage stimulation factor) binds a GU-rich sequence downstream of the cut site. They also bind Pol II, linking elongation to termination. Once the transcript is cleaved, poly-A polymerase adds a chain of ~200 adenines — the poly-A tail.

Label Key — making the tail
AAUAAA signal
Bound by CPSF; sits 10–30 nt upstream of the cut.
GU-rich sequence
Bound by CstF; downstream of the cut site, adding specificity.
Cleavage site
Where the transcript is cut; the downstream fragment is degraded in the nucleus.
Poly-A (~200 A)
Added by poly-A polymerase to the new 3' end.

The tail is not decoration: it increases transcript stability and allows export of the mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.

Label Key — the finished mRNA
5' cap (G-CH₃ + PPP)
Protective, ribosome-recruiting cap at the front.
Spliced body (exons only)
Introns removed; start and stop codons now sit in a continuous coding sequence.
Poly-A tail (150–250 A)
Stabilising, export-enabling tail at the back.
Clinical / real-world · when processing goes wrong

Because splice sites are so short and precise, a single base change can wreck them. Many cases of β-thalassaemia arise from mutations at β-globin splice sites that cause introns to be retained or exons skipped, so no functional globin is made. The therapeutic flip side: the drug nusinersen for spinal muscular atrophy is an antisense oligonucleotide that redirects splicing of the SMN2 gene to include a needed exon — processing biology turned into medicine.

R Recall — processing
  • 5' cap — 7-methylguanosine at ~25 nt via 5'-5' link; IDs mRNA, protects it, recruits ribosome.
  • Splicing — spliceosome removes introns (GU…A…AG) via branching + exon ligation; alternative splicing = diversity.
  • Poly-A — CPSF (AAUAAA) + CstF (GU-rich) → cleave → ~200 A; stability + export.
§5Part III · the code

The genetic code & tRNA

How a four-letter nucleic-acid alphabet is decoded into a twenty-letter protein alphabet.

Translation is the synthesis of protein from RNA — nucleotides read out as amino acids. The mRNA is read sequentially, three bases at a time; each triplet is a codon. With four bases in groups of three there are 4³ = 64 codons — plenty to specify the 20 common amino acids.

§5.1The code is redundant

Of the 64 codons, 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). Because 61 codons cover only 20 amino acids, the code is redundant (degenerate): a single amino acid may be specified by anywhere from 1 to 6 different codons (Plate 5.1).

Label Key — reading the table
Columns of codons
All the triplets that specify one amino acid sit together — often 2, 4 or 6 per amino acid.
Three-letter / one-letter names
e.g. Arg = R, His = H — the standard amino-acid abbreviations.
"stop"
UAA, UAG, UGA — no amino acid; ends the chain.

§5.2Transfer RNA — the adaptor

Codons cannot grab amino acids directly; the adaptor that reads a codon and carries the matching amino acid is transfer RNA (tRNA) — a small RNA (~80 nt) that folds into a cloverleaf in 2-D and an L-shape in 3-D (Plate 5.2). Two regions do the work: the anticodon (three bases that pair with the mRNA codon) and the 3' amino-acid attachment site.

Label Key — parts of a tRNA
Anticodon
Three consecutive bases in the anticodon loop that base-pair with the complementary codon on the mRNA.
3' acceptor stem
The 3' end where the correct amino acid is attached.
Cloverleaf (2-D) / L-shape (3-D)
The same molecule drawn flat vs folded; the fold brings anticodon and amino acid to opposite ends of the L.

§5.3Wobble

There are not 61 different tRNAs. Accurate base-pairing is required only at the first two codon positions; at the third position a mismatch — a wobble — can be tolerated (the wobble must be between a purine and a pyrimidine). So one tRNA can read several codons. Humans have >500 tRNA genes representing 48 anticodons. Plate 5.3 shows a single Ser tRNA reading more than one codon.

Label Key — how wobble works
Positions 1 & 2
Strict Watson–Crick pairing — this fixes which amino acid is read.
Position 3 (wobble)
Loosely paired; a purine–pyrimidine mismatch is allowed, so one anticodon covers several codons.
Pseudouridine (Ψ)
One of the modified bases found in tRNA loops.
Reasoning · why wobble is efficient, not sloppy

Wobble is not a flaw — it is the reason the cell can manage with ~48 anticodons instead of 61 tRNAs. Because redundant codons for one amino acid usually differ only at the third base (§5.1), allowing looseness there lets a single tRNA cover a whole codon family without ever changing which amino acid is inserted. Strictness where it matters (positions 1–2), tolerance where it doesn't (position 3): a neat economy.

§5.4Charging a tRNA

Each tRNA is charged with its correct amino acid by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase. There are 20 — one per amino acid — and each recognises its amino acid and all the tRNAs compatible with it, reading the anticodon loop and 3' stem and using ATP (Plate 5.4). The amino acid is joined to the tRNA by a high-energy bond; that stored energy later drives peptide-bond formation.

Label Key — charging
tRNA synthetase
The enzyme (here tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase); grips the correct amino acid, ATP and tRNA.
Anticodon stem & 3' acceptor stem
The two tRNA regions the enzyme reads to confirm identity.
ATP → AMP + 2Pᵢ
Energy source; drives formation of the high-energy amino-acid–tRNA bond.
High-energy bond
The activated linkage that will later pay for peptide-bond formation.

Amino acids are then joined by peptide bonds — between the carboxyl (C-) group of the growing chain and the free amino (N-) group of the incoming amino acid — so a protein is always built from its N-terminus to its C-terminus.

Clinical / real-world · errors in the code

Because codons are read exactly, single-base mutations translate straight into disease: a missense change swaps one amino acid (sickle-cell anaemia — Glu→Val in β-globin), while a nonsense change creates a premature stop codon and a truncated protein (many cases of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis). Mutations in mitochondrial tRNAs — which have their own small set — cause syndromes such as MELAS and MERRF, hitting energy-hungry tissues hardest.

R Recall — code & tRNA
  • Code — 64 codons; 61 code amino acids, 3 stop; redundant (1–6 codons/aa).
  • tRNA — ~80 nt, cloverleaf/L; anticodon + 3' amino-acid site.
  • Wobble — strict at positions 1–2, loose at 3; 48 anticodons suffice.
  • Charging — 20 synthetases, ATP, high-energy bond; protein grows N→C.
§6Part III · translation

Translation — the ribosome in action

The machine that reads the message: initiation, elongation, termination.

Protein synthesis happens on the ribosome, a machine built from more than 50 proteins and several ribosomal RNA (rRNA) species. A typical cell holds millions of them; at ~25 nm across, ~10,000 could fit inside a printed full stop. Some float free in the cytosol, others dock on the endoplasmic reticulum.

§6.1Ribosome structure

The large (60S) and small (40S) subunits are assembled in the nucleolus, exported, and join on an mRNA near its 5' end to form the 80S ribosome. There are four key regions: the mRNA-binding site and three tRNA sites — A, P and E (Plate 6.1).

Label Key — the ribosome
Large subunit (60S)
Contains 28S, 5.8S and 5S rRNA plus ~50 proteins; houses the catalytic peptidyl-transferase and the tRNA sites.
Small subunit (40S)
Contains 18S rRNA plus ~35 proteins; binds the mRNA and monitors codon–anticodon pairing.
A site (aminoacyl)
Binds the incoming charged tRNA carrying the next amino acid.
P site (peptidyl)
Holds the tRNA to which the growing polypeptide is attached.
E site (exit)
Where a spent tRNA leaves after donating its amino acid.
Reasoning · why 40S + 60S ≠ 100S

The "S" is a Svedberg unit — a measure of how fast a particle sediments in a centrifuge, which depends on both mass and shape, not mass alone. Larger, more compact particles sediment disproportionately faster, so the values are not additive: a 40S and a 60S subunit combine into an 80S ribosome, not 100S. Whenever you see "S", think "sedimentation rate", not "size you can add up".

§6.2Initiation

The 40S subunit teams up with three eukaryotic initiation factors (eIF) to form a preinitiation complex, which picks up the initiator tRNAMet (carrying methionine) and eIF5. With mRNA bound (via eIF4), the complex scans along the mRNA from the 5' end looking for the start codon — usually the first AUG, embedded in a consensus Kozak sequence (ACCAUGG). Finding it triggers recruitment of the 60S subunit to build the 80S ribosome; the eIFs then dissociate. The initiator tRNA sits in the P site, leaving the A site vacant for the second tRNA (Plate 6.2).

Label Key — initiation
Initiator tRNAMet
Carries methionine; lands in the P site (anticodon UAC reading AUG).
eIF1 / eIF1A / eIF3 / eIF4 / eIF5
Initiation factors that assemble the complex, bind the cap and drive scanning; they leave once the 80S forms.
Kozak sequence (ACCAUGG)
The context around the AUG that marks it as the real start codon.
Cap
The 5' cap where scanning begins.

§6.3Elongation

Elongation recruits elongation factors (EF) and repeats a three-step cycle, each step powered by GTP hydrolysis (Plate 6.3):

  1. Recruit a charged tRNA into the A site (codon–anticodon pairing checked here).
  2. Peptide bond forms between the amino acid in the A site and the growing chain in the P site.
  3. Translocation — the ribosome moves one codon in the 3' direction; the tRNAs shift P→E and A→P, and the spent tRNA exits.

It is fast and fairly accurate: about 15 amino acids per second in eukaryotes, with an error of roughly 1 in 104 amino acids.

Label Key — elongation
Incoming (charged) tRNA
Enters the A site carrying the next amino acid.
Growing polypeptide
Held in the P site; extended by each new peptide bond, read N→C.
Exiting (uncharged) tRNA
Leaves via the E site once its amino acid has been transferred.
Ribosome movement (5'→3')
Translocation shifts the ribosome one codon along the mRNA.

§6.4Termination

The cycle continues until a stop codon (UAG, UGA or UAA) reaches the A site. There is no tRNA with an anticodon for a stop codon; instead the release factor eRF1 binds the stop codon in the A site, the finished polypeptide is released, and the ribosome subunits separate (Plate 6.4).

Label Key — termination
Stop codon in A site
UAG/UGA/UAA arrives; no matching tRNA exists.
eRF1 (+ GTP)
The release factor that recognises the stop codon and triggers release.
Released polypeptide
The finished protein, freed from the last tRNA; the ribosome then dissociates.

§6.5Polyribosomes & the bigger picture

  • Polyribosomes — many ribosomes translate one mRNA at the same time (seen as strings on electron micrographs), so each message is used efficiently.
  • Not coupled — in eukaryotes transcription (nucleus) and translation (cytoplasm) are separated in space and time; the pre-mRNA is fully processed before export.
  • One message, one polypeptide — each mRNA directs the synthesis of a single kind of protein.
Clinical / real-world · antibiotics hit the ribosome

Bacterial ribosomes (70S = 50S + 30S) differ enough from our 80S that many antibiotics can block them selectively: aminoglycosides and tetracyclines jam the small subunit, macrolides (e.g. erythromycin) block the large-subunit exit tunnel. Diphtheria toxin, by contrast, poisons our own elongation factor. And a premature stop codon from a nonsense mutation ends translation early — the mechanism behind many severe genetic diseases and the target of "read-through" drugs.

R Recall — translation
  • Ribosome — 40S + 60S → 80S; A (incoming), P (peptide), E (exit); S = sedimentation, not additive.
  • Initiation — 40S + eIFs + tRNA-Met scan from cap to first AUG (Kozak) → 60S joins → 80S.
  • Elongation — A→peptide bond→translocate; GTP-powered; ~15 aa/s.
  • Termination — stop codon → eRF1 (no tRNA) → release + dissociate.
R Recall checklist — Gene Expression end to end
  • Central dogma — DNA → RNA → protein; RNA built 5'→3'; U replaces T.
  • Gene layout — promoter, TSS, exons/introns, UTRs; AUG start, UAA/UAG/UGA stop; template vs coding strand.
  • RNA polymerases — no primer, modest proofreading; Pol I (rRNA), II (mRNA), III (tRNA/5S).
  • Initiation — core promoter builds the PIC (Pol II + TBP + GTFs); TFIIH opens DNA + phosphorylates Pol II.
  • Processing — 5' cap, spliceosome (branching + exon ligation), poly-A tail (CPSF/CstF → ~200 A).
  • Code & tRNA — 64 codons (61 + 3 stop), redundant; tRNA anticodon + charged by synthetases; wobble at position 3.
  • Translation — 80S ribosome, A/P/E; scan to AUG → elongate (GTP) → stop codon + eRF1 release; protein built N→C.

Built from: MEDI2200 Week 6 — Gene Expression Parts I–III (RNA & RNA Polymerases · Transcription · Translation), Prof. Helen Rizos, Macquarie University. Personal study aid using the lecture's own figures.
